blocks.text: A question answer dataset pairs a question with the correct answer, sometimes alongside a piece of supporting context, the standard shape for fine-tuning a model to answer questions accurately rather than just complete text plausibly.

This topic covers how to structure these examples well, the difference between extractive and generative answering, and the practical challenges around unanswerable questions and multiple valid answers.
1. What a Question Answer Dataset Looks Like

blocks.alt: What a Question Answer Dataset Looks Like
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359107-924402115.png

At minimum, a QA example needs a question and a correct answer. Many QA datasets also include a context passage, the source material the answer should be grounded in, which is especially important for fine-tuning a model to answer based on supplied information rather than its own possibly outdated internal knowledge.
2. Extractive vs Generative Question Answering
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359108-99633796.png
Extractive question answering pulls the answer directly as a span of text from a given context passage, useful when the answer is guaranteed to exist verbatim somewhere in the source material.

Generative question answering produces a newly written answer, which may paraphrase, summarize, or synthesize information from the context rather than quoting it directly, and is the more common shape for modern decoder based fine-tuning.

blocks.text: 3. Where the Answer Comes From
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359108-776885295.png

For extractive style datasets, the answer needs to be traceable to an exact location in the source document, which usually means recording both the answer text and its position, so the training data reflects a genuine, verifiable extraction rather than an approximate paraphrase.
4. Handling Questions With No Good Answer

blocks.alt: Handling Questions With No Good Answer
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359394-845901970.png

Real world QA systems inevitably face questions the available context cannot actually answer. Deliberately including unanswerable examples, paired with a correct response acknowledging that the answer is not available, teaches the model to recognize and handle this case rather than confidently fabricating an answer.

blocks.title: Fabricated confident answers are a known failure mode
blocks.content: Without examples that teach a model to say the information is not available, a fine-tuned QA model tends to default toward producing a plausible sounding but incorrect answer instead.

blocks.text: 5. Multiple Valid Answers to the Same Question

blocks.alt: Multiple Valid Answers to the Same Question
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359395-374668629.png

Some questions genuinely have more than one acceptable answer, either because the source material supports several correct phrasings, or because the question itself is somewhat open ended. Where this is the case, including multiple accepted answers, or accepting some variation during evaluation, prevents a technically correct response from being unfairly marked wrong.
6. Context Length and QA Datasets
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359395-332503417.png

When context passages are long, approaching the model context window limit discussed in the Introduction module, care is needed to ensure the relevant answer bearing portion is not truncated away, or that training examples are deliberately built to test the model ability to find an answer buried in a longer passage.
7. Evaluating QA Fine-Tuning Quality

QA quality is typically evaluated by comparing generated answers against reference answers, sometimes using exact match, sometimes using a more flexible similarity based comparison to account for reasonable paraphrasing, a topic covered more fully in this course dedicated Evaluation module.
8. Building a QA Dataset From Existing Documentation

blocks.alt: Building a QA Dataset From Existing Documentation
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785448359396-607513019.png

A practical way to bootstrap a QA dataset is generating candidate questions from existing documentation, using either a model or a structured process, then verifying each generated question against the source document before including it in the final dataset.
This connects directly back to the Synthetic Data Generation topic covered earlier in this course, applied specifically to the QA dataset shape.
9. Structuring for Multi-Document QA

Some QA tasks require synthesizing an answer across more than one source document rather than a single passage, a harder variant that needs its own dataset design, since the model must learn to combine information rather than locate it in one place.
Worked Example

A team fine-tuning a model to answer questions about their product documentation builds a dataset of four thousand question, context, answer triples, deliberately including three hundred unanswerable questions paired with a correct not available in the documentation response.

Without those unanswerable examples, an earlier version of the model had confidently invented plausible sounding but incorrect answers to questions the documentation simply did not cover, a problem the added examples specifically corrected.
Common Mistakes

items: Building a dataset with no unanswerable examples, encouraging the model to fabricate confident answers
Truncating context passages in a way that accidentally removes the actual answer bearing text
Treating a question with multiple valid phrasings as having only one acceptable correct answer
Mixing extractive and generative answer styles inconsistently within the same dataset without a clear reason

blocks.text: Practice

Take a short piece of documentation you have access to and write three question answer pairs from it, including at least one question the documentation genuinely does not answer, paired with an appropriate refusal response.
Key Takeaway

A well built question answer dataset pairs questions with correct, appropriately grounded answers, deliberately including unanswerable examples so the model learns to recognize the limits of its available context rather than fabricating a confident but incorrect response.
